readings.model_translation: The Savior said to the rich man: ‘Why were you so tenacious of my goods, which I gave you? Why did you neglect the gift that I gave you? I shall now deprive you of my bounty, which I granted you; then you will be a beggar in worldly life. Why would you not remember that I intend to repay every person for a good deed that one does for my name’s sake? I repay it to him a hundredfold, as it is stated and said in my gospel: Whatever you give to one of my least ones, you always give it to me, and in return for that I will give you eternal joy in heaven.’
readings.translation_punctuation_note: English quotation punctuation is editorial; the exact Old English transcript preserves the continuing outer quotation without an added closing mark.
essential_points: The speaker owns the goods and bestowed the gift; the rich man is charged with withholding/neglecting it.
Woruldlīfe is worldly life, the sense expressly given by Cook323; an afterlife interpretation is not imported.
Mann in the good-deed clause is the generic agent, one/a person, not a plural poor-people subject.
Mid hundtēontigum gives the hundredfold return; wið ðǣm gives exchange in return for that.
Drēam is joy/bliss; Cook159n11 expressly rejects dream.
defensible_alternatives: holding tightly to/withholding for fæsthafol, provided the genitive goods remain its complement
will repay for present forgielde in its promised future setting
in the heavens for on heofonum

readings.model_translation: King Alfred was the translator of this book and translated it from Latin into English, as it is now arranged. Sometimes he set word against word, sometimes sense against sense, as he could then explain it most clearly and intelligibly amid the various and manifold worldly cares that often occupied him both in mind and in body. The cares that came upon the kingdoms of which he had taken charge in his days are very hard for us to count. Nevertheless, when he had studied this book and translated it from Latin into an English account, he afterwards made it into verse, as it is now arranged. And now he asks and beseeches in God’s name each of those whom it may please to read this book to pray for him, and not to blame him if the reader understands it more correctly than Alfred could. For each person must, according to the measure of his understanding and according to his available leisure, say what he says and do what he does.
essential_points: Hīe/hēo consistently refers to the feminine book; Alfred is the translator.
The contrast is word-for-word versus sense-for-sense rendering.
The worldly cares constrained the clarity of his explanation; they did not prevent the translation altogether.
Hæfde governs both geleornod and gewęnd, with later versification as a separate action.
Bitt/hālsað have an understood Alfred subject as Cook162n4 directs.
The first hē in gif hē ... ðonne hē is the reader; the second is Alfred, expressly identified by notes6–7.
Lyste is impersonal; wīte is the verb blame, not the noun punishment.
defensible_alternatives: because of the ... cares for the causal for phrase
prose/account/discourse for spelle, without claiming that prose is its only lexical sense
had received for underfangen, provided its relation to governing kingdoms is clear

readings.model_translation: Lord, almighty God, Maker and Ruler of all creatures, I beseech you by your great mercy, by the sign of the holy cross, by Saint Mary’s virginity, by Saint Michael’s obedience, and by the love of all your saints and their merits, to guide me better than my conduct towards you has deserved. Guide me according to your will and for my soul’s benefit, better than I myself may know; establish my mind according to your will and for my soul’s benefit; strengthen me against the devil’s temptations; remove from me foul lust and all unrighteousness; protect me against my adversaries, visible and invisible; and teach me to do your will, so that I may love you fervently above all things, with pure thought and a pure body. For you are my Creator and my Redeemer, my Help, my Comfort, my Trust and my Hope. May praise and glory be yours now and ever, ever, ever, for ever without any end. Amen.
essential_points: Rōde depends on tācne as a genitive; the for phrase governs dative tācne.
Sanctæ Marian and Sancti Michaeles have supplied genitive function with mixed foreign-name forms; no invented productive Latin table is implied.
Gehīersumnesse means obedience, not intercession.
The first requested verb is subjunctive gewissie; following gewissa, gestaðela, gestranga, āfierr, gescield and tǣc are direct commands.
Both occurrences of mīnre sāwle are genitives dependent on dative ðearfe.
Āworhte is understood contextually as what the speaker’s conduct has earned/deserved; it is not a command or a claim of having created God.
Ðīnne willan is the object of wyrceanne, as Cook163n7 states.
The last titles retain trust/trēownes and hope/tōhopa as distinct nouns; Sīe expresses the concluding wish.
defensible_alternatives: need/good for ðearfe in the soul-benefit phrase
more favorably than I have deserved towards you for the first comparison, while retaining the guidance request
may there be praise and glory to you for Sīe ðē lof and wuldor

independence_limit: This reconciled translation was prepared after source readings and colleagues’ independently frozen witness questions were discussed. It is not presented as a blind independent review or used to replace those witnesses.
